title: Designing the Widest Gothic Nave: Structural Logic and Geometric Ingenuity in Girona Cathedral
content: The Cathedral of Santa Maria of Girona represents one of the most daring structural enterprises in Gothic architecture, featuring the widest stone-vaulted nave ever constructed—an uninterrupted span of 22.98 meters. This architectural feat challenged conventional medieval design principles, which typically relied on dense forests of columns and flying buttress systems to manage lateral thrusts. Instead, the builders of Girona opted for a radical solution based on empirical knowledge, proportional design, and geometric intuition. This study investigates the structural logic behind this singular achievement, focusing on the application of the Rule of the Central Third, a geometric principle that guided medieval builders in maintaining thrust containment within masonry profiles. Combining historical sources, geometric reasoning, and physical modeling, the article reconstructs the structural behavior of the nave and buttress system using thrust line analysis and manual verification techniques. A scaled experimental model using wool thread and sectional drawings replicates the intuitive processes likely used by master builders to verify structural stability. The findings demonstrate that Girona Cathedral adheres remarkably well to the Rule of Thirds, validating the empirical intelligence embedded in its design. Moreover, a comparative analysis with other European Gothic cathedrals underlines Girona’s uniqueness not only in scale but also in structural strategy. Beyond historical analysis, the study offers insights for contemporary heritage conservation. It argues that preserving the original geometric logic and massing is essential for maintaining the building’s equilibrium. The case of Girona illustrates how empirical design, when grounded in proportion and form, can achieve structural performance equal to or exceeding modern expectations.
